title: Multifunction Process Calibrator: 7 Powerful Field Uses
text:
Calibration

 Multifunction Process Calibrator: 7 Powerful Field Uses

 One handheld tool that measures, sources and simulates almost every signal an instrument technician meets in a plant.

 
 mA Source and Measure 
 RTD and Thermocouple 
 Pressure Modules 
 Loop Power 
 




 A multifunction process calibrator can measure and source current, voltage, resistance, frequency, temperature and pressure from one handheld unit. It replaces a bag full of separate meters and simulators during calibration and loop checks.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn what a multifunction process calibrator is, the signals it can measure and simulate, and how to use it for fast and accurate field calibration.


 
 
 
 What Is a Multifunction Process Calibrator?


 A multifunction process calibrator is a portable, battery powered instrument with two independent channels that can measure one signal while sourcing another. Technicians use it to check transmitters, switches, indicators and control system inputs against a known reference, as explained in instrument calibration terms .


 Popular examples include the Fluke 725 and Fluke 726, along with similar models from Beamex, Additel and others. They are the everyday workhorse of most instrument maintenance teams.


 
 
 Image credit: Fluke 
 

 On the Fluke 726, the DC current range is 24 mA with accuracy of 0.01 percent plus 2 µA. Its voltage range is 30 V with accuracy of 0.01 percent plus 2 mV.


 It also measures resistance up to 4000 ohms and frequency up to 15 kHz. With external 750P modules, pressure accuracy reaches 0.025 percent.


 Measure, Source and Simulate Functions


 
 Measure Channel Reads mA, V, ohms, frequency and temperature

 Source Channel Outputs mA, V, ohms, frequency or TC signals

 Loop Power Built in 24 V supply for 2 wire transmitters

 Pressure Module External sensor for pressure measurement

 Result Memory Stores calibration results for reports




 Source mode drives a known signal into a device, such as 12 mA into a control valve positioner. Simulate mode acts like a 2 wire transmitter , controlling loop current supplied by the DCS.


 Measure mode reads the output of the device under test. Because both channels work together, you can source an input and read the output at the same time.


 The Fluke 726 loop supply provides 24 V with up to 22 mA. That is enough to power a transmitter on the bench without a separate power supply.


 7 Powerful Field Uses of a Multifunction Process Calibrator


 
 1
 Transmitter Calibration
 Apply a known input and read the mA output to find errors.


 2
 Loop Checks
 Simulate 4, 12 and 20 mA to verify DCS or PLC indication.


 3
 RTD Simulation
 Simulate Pt100 resistance to test temperature inputs.


 4
 Thermocouple Simulation
 Source millivolts with cold junction compensation for J, K, T and E types.


 5
 Pressure Switch Testing
 Capture set point and reset point with deadband.


 6
 Valve Positioner Checks
 Source mA and confirm valve travel response.


 7
 Frequency and Pulse
 Source pulses to test flow totalizers and counters.





 Use 2 is covered in detail in our instrument loop checking procedure . Use 5 connects well with pressure switch set point and deadband testing.


 Auto step and auto ramp functions speed up these jobs. The calibrator steps through 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent by itself while you watch the response.


 Transmitter Error Formula With a Worked Example


 
 Expected mA = 4 + 16 × (Input minus LRV) ÷ (URV minus LRV) 
 Error percent of span = (Measured mA minus Expected mA) ÷ 16 × 100 

Worked example:
Range 0 to 10 bar, applied input 5 bar
Expected mA = 4 + 16 × (5 ÷ 10) = 12.00 mA
Measured mA = 12.04 mA
Error = (12.04 minus 12.00) ÷ 16 × 100
 Error = 0.25 percent of span 



 Many multifunction calibrators calculate this error automatically in transmitter error mode. You only enter the range and the calibrator shows the error for each test point.


 If the error exceeds tolerance, perform a zero and span adjustment or a sensor trim, then repeat the as left test.


 Types of Process Calibrators


 
 Multifunction Calibrator
 Measures and sources electrical, temperature and pressure signals.
 Best for: general instrument maintenance
 All Round 

 Documenting Calibrator
 Adds HART communication and automatic result upload.
 Best for: large plants with calibration software
 Paperless 

 Loop Calibrator
 Focused on mA source, simulate and measure only.
 Best for: quick loop checks
 Compact 

 Temperature Calibrator
 Specialized RTD and thermocouple simulation and measurement.
 Best for: temperature heavy plants
 Temperature 




 For sensor level temperature calibration you still need a heat source such as a dry block calibrator . The multifunction unit reads the sensor while the block holds a stable temperature.


 Our guide on types of temperature calibrators explains how these tools work together. Documenting models that talk HART still need the proper loop resistance described in HART loop resistor basics.


 Choosing between these types depends on plant size and how results are recorded. Small teams often start with a basic handheld unit and move to documenting models when audits demand paperless records.


 Calibrator Comparison Table


 
 
 Tool Electrical Signals Temperature Pressure Best Use 

 Multifunction calibrator Yes Simulate and measure With modules Field calibration 

 Loop calibrator mA only No No Loop checks 

 Dry block No Generates heat No Sensor calibration 

 Dead weight tester No No Primary standard Pressure reference 

 



 A dead weight tester remains the reference for high accuracy pressure work. The multifunction unit is faster and more practical in the field.


 Most technicians carry a multifunction calibrator and a hand pump together. That pair covers the majority of daily calibration jobs.
